title: Axolotls can regrow a lost leg, and even parts of their heart and brain
body: The axolotl is a Mexican salamander that never grows up: it keeps its feathery external gills and stays in the water for life, a state called neoteny. It can regenerate entire limbs and its tail, and even parts of its eyes, heart and brain, which is why laboratories around the world study it. Its genome, published in 2018, holds about **32 billion base pairs**, roughly ten times as many as ours, yet it codes for a similar number of proteins. In the wild it survives only in the canals of Lake Xochimilco near Mexico City and is critically endangered.

cover.alt: Two pale leucistic axolotls with pink feathery gills resting on sand among aquarium plants

slides.prompt: Surveys counted about 6,000 axolotls per km² in Lake Xochimilco, near Mexico City, in 1998. How many per km² did they find in 2008?
slides.detail: The density fell from about 6,000 per km² in 1998 to 1,000 in 2003 and 100 in 2008. A four-month search in 2013 found none at all, then two turned up a month later.

slides.heading: Axolotls counted per km² of Lake Xochimilco
slides.note: The wild population is estimated at roughly 50 to 1,000 adults; critically endangered

slides.heading: Genome size, relative to a human's
slides.note: About 32 billion base pairs, roughly ten times ours, yet a similar number of protein-coding genes

slides.alt: A dark olive wild-type axolotl with bushy reddish external gills walking on sand in an aquarium
slides.caption: A wild-type axolotl. The bushy external gills are a larval feature that it keeps for its whole life.

slides.heading: Why it never grows up
slides.text: Most salamanders lose their gills and move onto land. Laboratory and pet axolotls lack the thyroid-stimulating hormone needed to trigger the thyroxine that drives metamorphosis, so they reach sexual maturity still looking like larvae, gills and all.

slides.heading: Axolotl: fact or myth?
